It is not the vocabulary that stops me. It is the speed.
It was the tone of the editorial that surprised me.
What slows me down is everything the sentence does not say.
All I want is one good article a week, not a hundred pages.
You have had that page open for twenty minutes. Is it the language?
It is not the language, actually. What slows me down is everything the sentence decides not to say.
Then you are reading it correctly. Half of a piece like that is implication.
Twelve pages in, and I still could not tell you what the writer actually thinks.
The editorial is where the opinion lives, and it carries no name at the bottom on purpose. Everything after it is reporting.
So what I should do is skim the whole thing first, and then choose one piece.
One piece, properly. It was that habit that got me through twenty years of it, and I was paid to read.
What surprises me is that nobody ever told me I was allowed not to finish.
What struck me about the piece was the tone.
It is not the vocabulary that stops me, it is the speed.
All I want is one good article a week.
The reason I stopped is that I thought I had to finish it.
It was the last paragraph that changed my mind.

Good morning, and welcome to the audio edition for the week of the ninth. Three things before we start the sections. Our correspondent in Ankara has filed the briefing this week, and it runs a little longer than usual, so the finance pages have moved back by four. The editorial takes a position that some of you are not going to like, and we know that, because we ran a version of the same argument in March and the letters came in for a month. And finally, a correction. Last week we said the vote was on the twelfth. It was on the twenty-first. The error was ours and not the correspondent's, and we apologize for it.

Here is what actually works with a difficult article, and it takes twenty minutes a week rather than an hour a day. Start at the end. Read the last paragraph first, because in this kind of writing the last paragraph is where the argument lands, and once you know where you are going the middle stops being a fog. Then go back to the top and skim, not for meaning but for shape. The names, the numbers, the two or three words that come back three times. Only now read it properly, and while you read, keep one question in your head. What is this writer trying to make me believe? Then mark one sentence you disagree with, even slightly. That one sentence is the thing you will be able to say out loud at a table on Friday, and saying it is the whole point. Finishing the magazine is not.
